title: Moby-Dick
author: Herman Melville
setting: New Bedford and Nantucket, then the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific whaling grounds, in the 1840s
lengthNote: One hundred and thirty-five chapters and an epilogue, with two compilations of quotation and word-history standing in front of the narrative
summary: A schoolmaster with no money and a damp November in his soul signs on to a Nantucket whaler, and finds that the captain means to spend the voyage hunting the white whale that took his leg. Melville keeps interrupting the chase with sermons, stage directions, dictionary entries and a whole natural history of the animal, so that the book acquires the shape of Ishmael's mind rather than Ahab's. Everyone aboard dies except the man telling the story, and he survives on a coffin.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Moby-Dick
sourceText.note: References give the chapter. The text follows the American edition, which carries the epilogue the London issue left out.

atAGlance.label: London first
atAGlance.note: Richard Bentley printed it in three volumes as The Whale, expurgated, and without the epilogue.

atAGlance.label: New York first
atAGlance.note: Harper & Brothers printed it in one volume as Moby-Dick; or, The Whale.

atAGlance.label: Dedication
atAGlance.note: Inscribed in token of his genius; the two men were neighbours in the Berkshires while the book was being finished.

atAGlance.label: Chief sources
atAGlance.note: A whaleship sunk by a sperm whale in 1820, and a white bull already famous in maritime print.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Some run to twenty pages; several run to less than one.

structure.label: Chapters 1–22
structure.title: New Bedford, Nantucket, and a bargain made in bed
structure.summary: Ishmael goes to sea to keep himself from stepping into the street and knocking people's hats off. He shares a bed with a tattooed harpooneer, hears Father Mapple preach on Jonah from a pulpit shaped like a ship's bow, and signs articles with two Quaker owners who haggle over his lay while Ahab stays below, unseen.

scenes.title: Loomings
scenes.summary: Ishmael explains why water draws landsmen to the ends of piers, and why he ships as a sailor rather than a passenger.

scenes.title: The Spouter-Inn
scenes.summary: A night of terror at sharing a bed with a cannibal ends in the calmest sleep Ishmael has had.

scenes.title: The Sermon
scenes.summary: Father Mapple makes Jonah a story about flight, punishment and obedience, and preaches it to men about to sail.

scenes.title: The Ship
scenes.summary: Peleg and Bildad bargain over Ishmael's share of the profits and let slip that the captain is not himself.

structure.label: Chapters 23–40
structure.title: The oath that changes the voyage
structure.summary: The Pequod clears the harbour on Christmas Day with the captain invisible. When Ahab finally appears he nails a gold doubloon to the mast, tells the crew what the voyage is actually for, and has them drink to the death of the white whale. Starbuck objects once, on the record, and is overruled by a speech.

scenes.title: Knights and Squires
scenes.summary: Starbuck is introduced as a man whose courage is an instrument rather than a temperament.

scenes.title: The Quarter-Deck
scenes.summary: Ahab nails up the doubloon, names the whale, and turns a business voyage into a private war.

scenes.title: Sunset
scenes.summary: Alone in the cabin, Ahab describes his own will as rolling stock on rails it cannot leave.

scenes.title: Midnight, Forecastle
scenes.summary: The crew sings and quarrels in a scene printed as a play, with stage directions and no narrator.

structure.label: Chapters 41–47
structure.title: What the whale is, and what white means
structure.summary: The narrative stops to explain the enemy. Ishmael gathers the rumours that make Moby Dick ubiquitous and immortal, sets out Ahab's transfer of every grievance onto one animal, and then devotes a whole chapter to the colour white, which he cannot make mean anything and cannot make mean nothing.

scenes.title: Moby Dick
scenes.summary: The whale's reputation is assembled out of sailors' talk, and Ahab's monomania is dated to the loss of his leg.

scenes.title: The Whiteness of the Whale
scenes.summary: Ishmael tries to explain why the colour frightens him and produces a chapter about the failure of symbols.

scenes.title: The Chart
scenes.summary: Ahab plots currents and seasons to predict where one animal will be in an ocean.

structure.label: Chapters 48–92
structure.title: The industry underneath the hunt
structure.summary: Boats are lowered, whales are killed, and the book becomes an account of work: the line coiled in tubs where one snag will take a man overboard, the cutting-in, the head hoisted against the rail, the blubber rendered down. Gams with other ships bring news, and each captain Ahab meets refuses or fails to give him what he wants.

scenes.title: The Line
scenes.summary: The whale-line is described as a thing that sits in loops around every man in the boat.

scenes.title: The Grand Armada
scenes.summary: Inside a panicked herd the boats drift into a calm centre where whales are nursing their young.

scenes.title: Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
scenes.summary: A rule of whaling property is extended, without comment, to nations, colonies and human beings.

structure.label: Chapters 93–110
structure.title: Pip overboard, the try-works alight, the coin read aloud
structure.summary: The cabin boy jumps from a boat and is left in the open sea long enough to lose his reason, which the book treats as a form of sight. Ishmael squeezes sperm until he loves everyone aboard, warns himself against staring into the try-works fire at night, and watches every officer in turn read the doubloon and find himself in it.

scenes.title: The Castaway
scenes.summary: Pip is abandoned in the water; the ship recovers a body and the crew decides the mind is gone.

scenes.title: A Squeeze of the Hand
scenes.summary: Working sperm back to liquid produces the most unguarded happiness in the book.

scenes.title: The Try-Works
scenes.summary: The ship rendering blubber at night looks like something sailing out of hell, and Ishmael nearly steers it onto a course by staring.

scenes.title: The Doubloon
scenes.summary: Ahab, Starbuck, Stubb, Flask, the Manxman, Queequeg, Fedallah and Pip each interpret the same coin.

structure.label: Chapters 111–132
structure.title: Compass, quadrant, coffin, calm
structure.summary: Ahab smashes the quadrant, remagnetises the compass needles after a typhoon, and refuses the Rachel's captain a day's search for his own lost son. The carpenter turns Queequeg's coffin into a life-buoy. In one clear morning Ahab asks Starbuck to let him look into a human eye, and then orders him to stay aboard.

scenes.title: The Candles
scenes.summary: St Elmo's fire burns at the mastheads and Ahab addresses the lightning as a personal acquaintance.

scenes.title: The Pequod Meets the Rachel
scenes.summary: A captain begs help searching for his missing boat and his son; Ahab refuses and sails on.

scenes.title: The Symphony
scenes.summary: Ahab weeps into the sea, wonders what is commanding him, and sends Starbuck away.

structure.label: Chapters 133–135 and the Epilogue
structure.title: Three days, and one man left
structure.summary: The whale is raised at last and fought for three days. It stoves the boats, drowns Fedallah in the lines, and finally runs at the ship itself and sinks it. Ahab goes down fastened to his own harpoon rope. Ishmael, thrown clear on the first day of the chase, floats out of the vortex on the coffin.

scenes.title: The Chase — Third Day
scenes.summary: The Pequod is holed and sinks with the sky-hawk nailed to her mast; Ahab is carried off by his own line.

scenes.title: Epilogue
scenes.summary: The narrator explains how he alone survived, and which ship picked him up.

characters.name: Ishmael
characters.summary: He signs on as an ordinary sailor and then takes over the book, interrupting the voyage to explain whale anatomy, quote Sir Thomas Browne and stage a scene as drama. His curiosity is what saves him from Ahab's kind of attention: he keeps wanting to know what things are, rather than what they mean about him.
characters.clue: He goes to sea whenever he finds himself pausing in front of coffin warehouses, and he ends the book afloat on one.

characters.name: Captain Ahab
characters.summary: A Nantucket whaling captain of forty years' experience who has decided that one animal is responsible for everything wrong with the universe. He is a brilliant manager of men and a competent navigator, and he uses both skills to convert thirty crew members and a hundred thousand dollars of other people's property into an instrument of revenge.
characters.clue: He walks on a leg carved from whale jaw, nails a gold coin to the mast, and will not take the reward of the hunt because he has already spent it.

characters.name: Starbuck
characters.summary: The only officer who states plainly that hunting one whale for revenge is blasphemy and bad business, and the only one with the standing to stop it. He is brave in a measured, professional way, thinks of his wife and child at Cape Cod, and once stands outside Ahab's cabin with a loaded musket and cannot fire it.
characters.clue: He will not have a man in his boat who is not afraid of a whale, and he is the one person aboard who says out loud that the voyage is madness.
traits: obedient past the point of use

characters.name: Queequeg
characters.summary: A tattooed South Sea islander who left home to learn Christian civilisation and concluded that it was not worth the trouble. He is the best workman aboard, rescues a man who has just insulted him, and has his coffin built while he is still able to climb into it and try the fit.
characters.clue: He sells shrunken heads in the street, sleeps with a tomahawk pipe, and has his whole history tattooed on a body he cannot read.

characters.name: Stubb
characters.summary: He kills whales with a pipe in his mouth and a joke running, and treats the whole voyage as an amusing arrangement that somebody else is responsible for. His good humour is the book's most unsettling moral position, because it is indistinguishable from not caring what happens to anyone.
characters.clue: He jokes his way through every lowering, smokes at the moment of the kill, and reads the gold coin as a comic almanac.

characters.name: Pip
characters.summary: A small Black cabin boy from Alabama who is put into a whaleboat, jumps twice, and is left alone on the surface of the Pacific for a time no one bothers to measure. What comes back is treated by the crew as an idiot and by the narrator as a witness, and he is the one person Ahab treats tenderly.
characters.clue: He jumped from a boat once too often, came back from the water saying things nobody wanted to hear, and ended up holding a mad captain's hand.

characters.name: Fedallah
characters.role: Ahab's own harpooneer, kept below until the first lowering
characters.summary: A Parsee smuggled aboard with a boat's crew of his own, who gives Ahab a prophecy built like the witches' riddles in a tragedy: two hearses, a hemp rope, and a promise that he will go before his captain. Every clause comes true in a way Ahab never considered.
characters.clue: He is hidden in the hold until the first whale is raised, and his prophecy about hearses and hemp is the only accurate forecast in the book.

characters.name: Moby Dick
characters.summary: Rumoured to be in several oceans at once and impossible to kill, he is also a large animal doing what large animals do when harpooned. The book will not decide between those two descriptions, and the refusal is the point: Ahab needs the first, Ishmael keeps producing evidence for the second.
characters.clue: A wrinkled brow, a crooked jaw and a white hump — and the only character in the book with no interior at all.

themes.name: Monomania
themes.summary: Ahab's condition is precisely named in the book: one idea has taken the place of every other, and the rest of the mind still works normally in its service. That is why he is so persuasive. The danger is not that he raves but that he can run a ship, read a chart and win an argument while doing it.
themes.development: Introduced as an injury in Chapter 41, exhibited as leadership on the quarter-deck, and finally described in Chapter 132 as something that commands him rather than something he wills.

themes.name: Knowledge and its failures
themes.summary: Ishmael classifies whales as if they were books, measures a skeleton, reads pictures, quotes authorities and admits at every stage that the system does not hold. The novel is an encyclopaedia that keeps publishing its own errata, and the joke is serious: the thing being described is the one thing that will not sit still for description.
themes.development: From the Etymology and Extracts before the story begins, through the mock-bibliographic Cetology of Chapter 32, to the flat statement in Chapter 86 that the whale's face cannot be read at all.

themes.name: Whiteness and meaning
themes.summary: A whole chapter is given to a colour, and it concludes that white terrifies because it is both the absence of colour and the sum of all colours. That is a statement about interpretation rather than about whales: the novel's central object is blank enough to hold whatever is put into it, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.
themes.development: Chapter 42 sets the problem; the doubloon in Chapter 99 turns it into a demonstration, with seven men reading one small object seven different ways.

themes.name: Work at sea
themes.summary: Before the Pequod is a symbol it is a factory. Melville itemises the lay system that pays a sailor in fractions, the tubs of line that can take a man's arm off, the stink of the try-works and the market price of oil. Ahab's revenge is only possible because he controls somebody else's capital and thirty men's wages.
themes.development: Established in the bargaining of Chapter 16, sustained through the cutting-in chapters, and turned political in Chapter 89, where the law of fast-fish and loose-fish is applied to empires.

themes.name: Fellowship
themes.summary: The warmest passages in the book are about shared work and shared beds: two strangers under one counterpane, a monkey-rope tying two lives together, a crew squeezing lumps of sperm until they are squeezing each other's hands. Against this the novel sets a captain who cannot bear to be looked at.
themes.development: Begins as comedy in the Spouter-Inn, becomes a working principle in the monkey-rope chapter, and reaches its clearest statement in Chapter 94 before the try-works puts the fire back.

themes.name: Fate, chance and free will
themes.summary: The book states the problem as a weaver's loom: necessity is the warp, free will the shuttle, chance the blow that settles where the thread lies. Ahab argues both sides of it in the same speech, insisting that nothing can swerve him and then asking who is doing the pushing.
themes.development: Set out as an image in Chapter 47, asserted as iron rails in Chapter 37, and undone in Chapter 132 when Ahab asks whether Ahab is Ahab.

techniques.name: Encyclopaedic digression
techniques.definition: Interrupting a narrative with technical, historical or taxonomic material presented straight.
techniques.inThisBook: Whole chapters on the whale's skin, its head, its tail and the pictures painted of it delay the plot for hundreds of pages, and the delay is the book's argument about how long it takes to know anything.

techniques.name: Dramatic form
techniques.definition: Passages set out as a play, with stage directions, soliloquies and asides.
techniques.inThisBook: From Chapter 36 onwards Ahab's speeches are printed as theatre, and Chapter 40 abandons the narrator entirely for a scene of song and quarrel on the forecastle.

techniques.name: The unstable symbol
techniques.definition: An object placed at the centre of a work whose meaning is never settled by it.
techniques.inThisBook: The doubloon is nailed to the mast and then read aloud by seven characters in succession, each of whom finds a portrait of himself in the same coin.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: Borrowing names, phrases and situations from earlier texts to stand behind the present one.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrator is named for an outcast in Genesis, the captain for a king of Israel condemned by a prophet, and the rescuing ship for a mother weeping for her children.

techniques.name: Prophecy and foreshadowing
techniques.definition: Early signs and predictions that the reader can only read correctly in retrospect.
techniques.inThisBook: Elijah on the wharf, Fedallah's two hearses, and a coffin built for a sick harpooneer that becomes the ship's life-buoy and then the last page's raft.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: Accumulating items in a list until the list itself produces an effect.
techniques.inThisBook: Ahab's enumeration of everything that maddens and torments piles clause on clause until the whale is holding the weight of the entire human record.

quotations.text: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago⁠—never mind how long precisely⁠—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.
quotations.context: The opening of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The imperative does not give a name, it proposes one, and the difference matters in a book where Ahab's name is a judgement and the whale's is a trade nickname. The dashes then bury the only concrete facts — no money, nothing to do — inside an aside, so that the voyage arrives sounding like a whim rather than the last resort it turns out to be.

quotations.text: Who ain’t a slave? Tell me that.
quotations.context: Explaining why he ships before the mast rather than as a passenger or an officer.
quotations.analysis: The question is a joke about taking orders, and in a book published in 1851 by a New York house it is also not a joke. Ishmael's cheerful universalising — everybody is somebody's servant, so the thump goes round — is the exact argument the novel dismantles later, when Chapter 89 puts real people under the law of loose-fish.

quotations.text: Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.
quotations.context: Getting into bed at the Spouter-Inn beside a stranger he has spent the evening dreading.
quotations.analysis: The sentence works by putting the two adjectives where the two nouns expect to be judged: it is sobriety and drunkenness that decide, not heathen and Christian. Ishmael has reasoned his way out of a terror in about four lines, and the speed of the reversal sets the pattern for a narrator who revises his categories whenever the evidence asks him to.

quotations.text: Delight is to him⁠—a far, far upward, and inward delight⁠—who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, ever stands forth his own inexorable self.
quotations.speaker: Father Mapple
quotations.context: The close of the sermon on Jonah, preached to a congregation of whalemen about to sail.
quotations.analysis: Mapple's sermon has spent twenty minutes on the duty of obedience and ends by blessing the man who stands against every authority on earth. Ahab will take the second half of that lesson and leave the first, which is why the sermon has to come before he appears: the book gives him his theology in a church, from a pulpit shaped like the bow of a ship.

quotations.text: No more my splintered heart and maddened hand were turned against the wolfish world. This soothing savage had redeemed it.
quotations.context: Sitting by the fire with Queequeg the morning after their first night in the same bed.
quotations.analysis: The cure for the November in his soul turns out to be one specific person rather than the sea at all, which quietly undoes the whole rationale of Chapter 1. Note that redemption is credited to a man Ishmael was ready to call a devil the night before, and that the verb is in the past perfect — it has already happened, before the narrator noticed.

quotations.text: But as in landlessness alone resides highest truth, shoreless, indefinite as God⁠—so, better is it to perish in that howling infinite, than be ingloriously dashed upon the lee, even if that were safety!
quotations.context: A six-paragraph chapter about a sailor named Bulkington, who is never mentioned again.
quotations.analysis: The shortest chapter in the book states the ethic the rest of it will test to destruction, and then deletes the character it was attached to. Bulkington exists to make the argument and disappear, which is Melville telling the reader early that this book will introduce people for the length of an idea.

quotations.text: “I will have no man in my boat,” said Starbuck, “who is not afraid of a whale.”
quotations.speaker: Starbuck
quotations.context: Ishmael's introduction of the first mate, before Ahab has appeared on deck.
quotations.analysis: Fear is being described as a professional qualification: the man who feels none has no instrument for measuring the danger. Placed ten chapters before the quarter-deck scene, the line also tells the reader exactly what will be wrong with Ahab's command, and exactly why Starbuck will lose the argument — his courage is a calculation, and calculations can be shouted down.

quotations.text: “Vengeance on a dumb brute!” cried Starbuck, “that simply smote thee from blindest instinct! Madness! To be enraged with a dumb thing, Captain Ahab, seems blasphemous.”
quotations.speaker: Starbuck
quotations.context: The one objection raised on deck after Ahab names the voyage's real purpose.
quotations.analysis: Starbuck's case is that the whale cannot be guilty because it cannot intend, and the word he reaches for is theological rather than commercial. That choice loses him the argument: by admitting the question is about God, he lets Ahab answer on the same ground, and the reply about striking the sun follows immediately.

quotations.text: All visible objects, man, are but as pasteboard masks. But in each event⁠—in the living act, the undoubted deed⁠—there, some unknown but still reasoning thing puts forth the mouldings of its features from behind the unreasoning mask. If man will strike, strike through the mask!
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: Answering Starbuck's objection in front of the assembled crew.
quotations.analysis: Ahab's metaphysics is stated as stage property: the world is scenery, and something is standing behind it. The argument only works if there is a face under the mask, and he concedes two sentences later that there may be nothing at all — then says it does not matter. That concession, made aloud and immediately abandoned, is the clearest evidence in the book that he knows what he is doing.

quotations.text: Talk not to me of blasphemy, man; I’d strike the sun if it insulted me.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: The same speech, in reply to Starbuck's word for the voyage.
quotations.analysis: The conditional is the whole trick: he does not claim to be equal to the sun, only to be willing. Ahab consistently wins arguments by shifting them from what is possible to what he is prepared to do, and a crew that has just been given grog and a gold coin is in no state to notice the substitution.

quotations.text: The path to my fixed purpose is laid with iron rails, whereon my soul is grooved to run.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: Alone in the cabin immediately after the quarter-deck scene, in a soliloquy printed with a stage direction.
quotations.analysis: He chooses the most modern image available in 1851 — a railway — to describe a fate he insists is his own. The metaphor concedes more than he means: rails are laid by somebody, and the thing that runs on them has no say in the route. Ninety chapters later he will ask outright who laid them.

quotations.text: All that most maddens and torments; all that stirs up the lees of things; all truth with malice in it; all that cracks the sinews and cakes the brain; all the subtle demonisms of life and thought; all evil, to crazy Ahab, were visibly personified, and made practically assailable in Moby Dick.
quotations.context: The narrator's account of how Ahab's injury became a metaphysics.
quotations.analysis: Six clauses beginning with 'all' pile up before the sentence will name its subject, so the reader feels the accumulation before learning where it is going. The operative word is 'assailable': the appeal of the whale is not that it is evil but that it can be reached with a harpoon, which is what abstract grievances cannot.

quotations.text: It was the whiteness of the whale that above all things appalled me.
quotations.context: The opening admission of the chapter Ishmael gives to a colour.
quotations.analysis: 'Appalled' still carried its root sense of being made pale, so the sentence quietly turns the reader white as it reports the whiteness. Ishmael also separates himself from Ahab here: the captain is frightened by malice, the narrator by a colour, and it is the narrator's fear that the book then spends a whole chapter failing to explain.

quotations.text: is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows⁠—a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink?
quotations.context: Near the end of the chapter on whiteness, after a long list of white things that are and are not terrible.
quotations.analysis: 'Blankness, full of meaning' is a contradiction stated as a fact, and it describes the novel's method as much as its subject. The whole chapter is built out of questions rather than assertions; Ishmael cannot get the colour to signify, and by refusing to force it he shows exactly what Ahab does when he decides the whale is an argument.

quotations.text: God help thee, old man, thy thoughts have created a creature in thee; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus; a vulture feeds upon that heart forever; that vulture the very creature he creates.
quotations.context: After a description of Ahab bursting from his cabin at night, driven out of his hammock by his own dreams.
quotations.analysis: The purpose has become a separate organism living inside the man who made it, which is a more precise account of obsession than any diagnosis of madness. Melville folds the Prometheus story in on itself: the punishment is not sent by the gods but manufactured by the sufferer, so the vulture and the thing it feeds on have the same author.

quotations.text: The sea had jeeringly kept his finite body up, but drowned the infinite of his soul.
quotations.context: After Pip is left alone in the open Pacific and eventually picked up by the ship.
quotations.analysis: The chiasmus of finite body and infinite soul turns a rescue into a drowning, and the adverb does the moral work: the sea is not indifferent here but mocking. Melville has made the one survival in the middle of the book a disaster, which is worth holding against the Epilogue, where survival is presented as the plainest of facts.

quotations.text: So man’s insanity is heaven’s sense; and wandering from all mortal reason, man comes at last to that celestial thought, which, to reason, is absurd and frantic; and weal or woe, feels then uncompromised, indifferent as his God.
quotations.context: Explaining what the crew mean when they call Pip mad.
quotations.analysis: The sentence reverses the crew's verdict without contradicting it: Pip is exactly what they say he is, and that is the qualification. What he has acquired is indifference, the same quality the novel has just attributed to God, which makes his madness a kind of promotion and the ship's diagnosis a failure of rank rather than of medicine.

quotations.text: Come; let us squeeze hands all round; nay, let us all squeeze ourselves into each other; let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.
quotations.context: Working congealed spermaceti back into liquid with the rest of the crew.
quotations.analysis: The verb is repeated until it stops being industrial and becomes affectionate, which is the whole movement of the chapter: a task performed for the oil market produces the book's frankest declaration of love. The sentence also rewrites a phrase of Lady Macbeth's about the milk of human kindness, replacing an accusation of softness with a recommendation.

quotations.text: Look not too long in the face of the fire, O man! Never dream with thy hand on the helm! Turn not thy back to the compass; accept the first hint of the hitching tiller; believe not the artificial fire, when its redness makes all things look ghastly.
quotations.context: After Ishmael, steering at night, falls asleep facing the try-works and nearly capsizes the ship.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives about steering are also three imperatives about reading, and the near-disaster is the only time the narrator endangers the Pequod himself. Set the advice beside Ahab, who has spent the voyage looking at nothing else: the novel offers the corrective just two chapters before the doubloon proves how little good corrections do.

quotations.text: And some certain significance lurks in all things, else all things are little worth, and the round world itself but an empty cipher, except to sell by the cartload, as they do hills about Boston, to fill up some morass in the Milky Way.
quotations.context: Ahab pausing at the doubloon nailed to the mainmast.
quotations.analysis: This is the case for symbolism stated by its most compromised witness, and the alternative he offers is commerce: either things mean, or they are gravel to be carted away. The chapter then has six other characters read the same coin, which demonstrates the opposite of what Ahab needs — that significance lurks everywhere and therefore settles nowhere.

quotations.text: Close! stand close to me, Starbuck; let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: On a calm morning three days before the chase, talking to his first mate about forty years at sea.
quotations.analysis: After a hundred chapters of addressing the sun, the lightning and a severed whale's head, he asks to look at a person, and finds his own wife and child reflected there. The reversal lasts about a page: the same speech ends by ordering Starbuck to stay aboard, so the one moment of contact is spent buying the mate's absence.

quotations.text: Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm?
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: The same conversation, a few sentences later.
quotations.analysis: The first question puts a name on both sides of the verb and gets no answer, which is what the punctuation is for — the comma keeps the two Ahabs from resolving into one. Ninety-five chapters after declaring his soul grooved to run, he asks who laid the rails, and the arm he cannot account for is the one that will throw the harpoon.

quotations.text: Towards thee I roll, thou all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with thee; from hell’s heart I stab at thee; for hate’s sake I spit my last breath at thee.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: His last words, thrown at the whale as the Pequod goes down behind him.
quotations.analysis: 'All-destroying but unconquering' is an accurate summary of the situation and a defeat dressed as a distinction: the whale wins and is granted no victory. Ahab keeps the second person throughout, so the final speech of the book is addressed to an animal, and the harpoon line he throws with it catches him round the neck and takes him under.

quotations.text: Now small fowls flew screaming over the yet yawning gulf; a sullen white surf beat against its steep sides; then all collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the narrative proper, after the ship has gone down.
quotations.analysis: The sea is given a burial cloth and then denied any interest in the burial; five thousand years is the biblical age of the world, so the closing measure is one the Pequod's Quaker owners would recognise. Every noun in the sentence is doing the same work — the surf is sullen, the gulf yawns — and none of them is mourning.

quotations.text: It was the devious-cruising Rachel, that in her retracing search after her missing children, only found another orphan.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the book, describing the ship that picks Ishmael up.
quotations.analysis: The rescue is written as a disappointment: the Rachel is looking for her own children and finds a stranger. Melville has already had Ahab refuse this captain a day's search in Chapter 128, so the last act of the novel is the ship he wronged saving the only man left, and the last word is a category rather than a name.

timeline.label: Herman Melville born in New York
timeline.detail: His father's business failed and died with him, and Melville's formal schooling ended early.

timeline.label: The whaleship Essex is sunk by a sperm whale
timeline.detail: Owen Chase's narrative of the wreck and its aftermath became one of the novel's central sources.

timeline.label: J. N. Reynolds publishes an account of Mocha Dick
timeline.detail: A white sperm whale of the Pacific, already famous in maritime print before Melville named one.

timeline.label: Melville sails from Fairhaven on the whaler Acushnet
timeline.detail: He deserted in the Marquesas eighteen months later, which gave him the material for his first book.

timeline.label: Typee makes him briefly famous
timeline.detail: A South Seas narrative sold as fact; the reading public wanted more of the same from him for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Melville moves to Arrowhead and meets Hawthorne
timeline.detail: The book he was already writing grew considerably longer and stranger during the friendship.

timeline.label: Published as The Whale in London and Moby-Dick in New York
timeline.detail: The London issue was expurgated, ran to three volumes, and omitted the epilogue, so its reviewers met a narrator who appeared not to have survived.

timeline.label: Pierre is published and the reviews turn hostile
timeline.detail: Melville's reputation as a writer of readable sea adventures did not survive the two books together.

timeline.label: Melville dies in New York
timeline.detail: He had spent nearly twenty years as a customs inspector on the docks, and left Billy Budd unpublished.

timeline.label: Raymond Weaver's biography opens the Melville revival
timeline.detail: The first full life of the writer, published thirty years after his death, made the case that the neglected books were the important ones.

timeline.label: Rockwell Kent's illustrated edition
timeline.detail: His black-and-white designs shaped how a generation of readers pictured the ship and the whale.

timeline.label: John Huston's film, written with Ray Bradbury
timeline.detail: Gregory Peck as Ahab fixed the popular version of the story as a chase with the cetology cut out.

places.name: New Bedford, Massachusetts
places.note: The whaling capital where Ishmael arrives too late for the packet, and meets Queequeg at the Spouter-Inn.

places.name: Nantucket
places.note: Where the Pequod is fitted out, and the island the novel credits with inventing the whale fishery.

places.name: Pittsfield, Massachusetts
places.note: Arrowhead, the farmhouse where Melville finished the book within sight of Mount Greylock.

places.name: Cape Horn
places.note: The passage into the Pacific, and the route Ahab took the day after his wedding.

places.name: Strait of Sunda
places.note: The narrow water between Java and Sumatra where the Pequod meets the Grand Armada.

places.name: The Japanese whaling ground
places.note: The Pacific cruising ground where the typhoon strikes and the final chase begins.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest line of the twentieth-century revival reads the Pequod as a working model of the republic — a multinational crew, a democratic argument about labour, and a leader who can persuade free men to sign away their interests.
criticalViews.counter: It tends to treat the cetology chapters as ballast, when they are the part of the book that refuses to let the ship become a symbol.

criticalViews.position: The book as a crisis of interpretation
criticalViews.summary: A reading grounded in the whiteness chapter and the doubloon: the novel is about the impossibility of fixing meaning, and Ahab's error is not cruelty but certainty.
criticalViews.counter: Taken far enough it makes every position in the book equivalent, which is hard to sustain against a narrative in which thirty men actually drown.

criticalViews.position: The book as a document of work and empire
criticalViews.summary: Recent criticism has concentrated on whaling as a global extractive industry — the lay system, the Pacific labour market, the traffic in bodies that Chapter 89 puts under the same law as fish.
criticalViews.counter: This reading can be impatient with Ahab's rhetoric, which is where most of the novel's energy actually is.

criticalViews.position: The book as a quarrel with providence
criticalViews.summary: Father Mapple's sermon, Ahab's addresses to the lightning and Pip's promotion to prophet make a sustained argument with Calvinist inheritance, conducted by a writer who could neither believe nor let it alone.
criticalViews.counter: It risks turning Ishmael into a theologian, when his most characteristic act is to change the subject to whale anatomy.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Moby-Dick a novel about Ahab?
essayQuestions.focus: Narrative attention, digression and who the book belongs to
plan: Count the ground: Ahab does not appear until Chapter 28 and is absent from most of the middle three hundred pages.
Use Chapters 32, 42 and 86 to show Ishmael pursuing a wholly different question from his captain's.
Turn on Chapter 41, where the narrator explains Ahab so thoroughly that the explanation displaces the man.
Test the counter-case with the dramatic chapters, where Ahab speaks without a narrator between him and the reader.
Close on the Epilogue: the survivor is the one who kept getting distracted.

essayQuestions.question: What does the novel do with the colour white?
essayQuestions.focus: Symbol, blankness and the limits of reading
plan: Set out the structure of Chapter 42: a list of white things that are terrible, then a list of white things that are not.
Note the grammar — the chapter is built from questions, and never issues a conclusion.
Compare the doubloon in Chapter 99, where seven readings of one object are given in sequence.
Ask what Ahab does differently, and why fixing a meaning is presented as an act of violence.
Weigh the ending: the surf is white, and the sea is indifferent to what that means.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the treatment of work in Moby-Dick.
essayQuestions.focus: The lay system, the try-works and the economics of the voyage
plan: Begin with Chapter 16 and the haggle over Ishmael's three-hundredth lay: the voyage is a speculation in which the crew are investors who cannot withdraw.
Use the line, the monkey-rope and the cutting-in chapters to show danger described as routine.
Read Chapter 94 as the point where labour produces fellowship rather than oil.
Set Chapter 89 beside all of this: the law of fast-fish and loose-fish is applied to serfs, republics and continents.
Conclude on Ahab, who can only afford his revenge because somebody else owns the ship.

essayQuestions.question: 'Ishmael survives because he is interested in everything, and Ahab dies because he is interested in one thing.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Attention, obsession and the shape of the narrative
plan: Establish the contrast structurally: the digressions belong to Ishmael, the soliloquies to Ahab.
Use Chapter 96 to complicate it — Ishmael, too, stares into a fire and nearly wrecks the ship.
Bring in Pip, whose attention is destroyed by the sea and who is the one person Ahab can bear.
Consider Starbuck as a third case: he sees clearly, objects once, and obeys.
Decide whether the Epilogue offers survival as a reward or simply as an accident with a coffin in it.

discussionQuestions: The whale appears in person in only three chapters out of a hundred and thirty-five. Why does Melville keep it offstage for so long?
Chapter 42 tries to explain why whiteness is frightening and fails. Is the failure a flaw or the point?
Ishmael tells us he alone survived, but he narrates scenes he could not have witnessed. Does that damage the book?
Starbuck stands outside Ahab's cabin with a loaded musket and does not use it. What is the novel saying about conscience that stops short of action?
Is Pip mad, or is he the only character who has seen the thing the book is about?
The Pequod's crew comes from four continents and obeys one man without much argument. What does the novel think about that?

related.why: The book Moby-Dick is dedicated to its author, published the year before, and the other great American argument about a symbol nobody can fix.
The other study of a man whose thoughts create a creature that then feeds on him.
The poem behind Ahab's quarrel with heaven, and the source of the grandeur his speeches borrow.
The long sea voyage as a form, and the case of a captain who does get his crew home — most of them.
The other American book built on water, in which a narrator's voice matters more than the plot he is carrying.
